He further submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge has ignored the clear admission of the master of the ship that the carrier will be responsible for the loss, which is very crystal clear from the correspondences between the appellant and the respondent No. 2 and, as such, the averments made by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 that the claim is apparently time barred is not sustainable in law, which the learned Judge failed to accede, as such, the judgment and decree passed upon wrong computation of limitation of time makes those not sustainable and are liable to be reversed. 

 21. He also submitted that the learned trial Court Judge gravely erred by holding that the case was not filed within one year from 18-9-1975, in as much as, the plaintiff appellant conclusively proved and it was admitted by respondents that there are loss of cargo at the port due to negligence of the carrier, as such, the limitation of the suit is governed by Articles 115 of the Limitation Act, 1908 as during the whole period the parties were negotiating for the claim of the plaintiff, even long after the discharge of the cargo, as such, the special limitation provided by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act is not attracted, as such, the judgment upon misdirection is liable to be reversed. 

 22. He further asserted that there was a novation of the contract as the captain of the ship undertook to pay the damages independent of the B/L, as such, the failure on the part of the defendant respondents instituting the suit falls within purview of Articles 115 of the Limitation Act, as such, dismissal of the suit holding that the same is barred by limitation is unwarranted and prayed for allowing the appeal. 

 26. On point of limitation it is clearly encompassed in the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1924. The instant case, as per terms of the B/L the laws of England shall prevail however, the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925, applicable in Bangladesh also have the same provision in Article III rule 6 that any suit for damage be brought within 1(one) year from the date of delivery of the consignment. Article- III, rule 6 of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1924, which read as follows: "...Unless notice of loss or damage and the general nature of such loss or damage be given in writing to the carrier or his agent at the port of discharge before or at the time of the removal of the goods into the custody of the person entitled to delivery there-of under the contract of carriage, or, if the loss or damage be not apparent, within three days, such removal shall be prima facie evidence of the delivery by the carrier of the goods as described in the bill of lading. 

 30. The plaint clearly asserted that the cause of action being dated 31-12-1973 and the instant case was filed on 30-12-1976. On the other hand, Article-30, to the First Schedule of the Limitation Act, 1908, also has prescribed the same time limit therefore i.e. 1 (one) year for bringing any suit against a carrier for compensation for loss or injury to goods. Therefore, we find the suit being measurably time barred.
